lead: CYK answers one question: is a given string w in the language of a context-free grammar? It needs the grammar in Chomsky normal form: every rule is A → BC with B, C variables, or A → a with a a terminal. CNF also allows the extra rule S → ε, where S is the start variable. CYK as described handles |w| ≥ 1. For w = ε, check separately: it is in L(G) exactly when S → ε is a rule. The algorithm fills a table of sets of variables for every substring of w. Each cell reuses smaller cells, like a dynamic-programming table. Membership costs about n³·|P| rule checks for |w| = n and |P| rules; for a fixed grammar this is O(n³). Compiler and parser courses use it as a clean membership test; only a few universities teach it in detail.

blocks.text: Write w as s[1]...s[n]; s[i..j] is the substring from position i to j. V[i,j] holds every variable that derives s[i..j]. For length 1, A ∈ V[i,i] when A → s[i] is a rule. For length ℓ = j − i + 1 ≥ 2, try each split k from i to j−1. A ∈ V[i,j] if some rule A → BC has B ∈ V[i,k] and C ∈ V[k+1,j]. This is dynamic programming: each larger substring uses smaller ones. Accept w when S ∈ V[1,n]. |P| is the number of rules and |V| is the number of variables. Fill by increasing ℓ. CNF may also allow the extra rule S → ε; CYK as described covers |w| ≥ 1, so test w = ε separately. No other rule shapes are tried.
V[i,j] = ⋃ over k = i to j−1 of { A : A → BC, B ∈ V[i,k], C ∈ V[k+1,j] }
blocks.where: V[i,j] is the set of variables deriving s[i..j]; k is the split point; B and C are variables from the two parts; A is the left side of a CNF rule.

blocks.text: Start with all length-1 cells. Then fill length 2, length 3, up to n. A cell of length ℓ reads only cells of smaller lengths, so this order is safe. You can draw the n × n upper triangle, or rows of increasing length; both show the same cells. Store sets, not single variables, because several variables may derive one substring. The cell (i,j) covers exactly j−i+1 characters. Time is O(n³·|P|): n² cells, up to n splits, |P| rules. Space is O(n²·|V|). The answer is V[1,n], not the last cell you happen to fill. A parse tree can be recovered by keeping back-pointers for each split that added a variable. If S is absent from V[1,n], w is not in L(G). Empty cells mean no variable derives that substring. CYK is a decision test; it says yes or no. It does not list all derivations.

examples.question: Grammar G: S → AB, A → AA | a, B → b. Test whether w = aab belongs to L(G) using CYK. Give V[1,1], V[2,2], V[3,3], V[1,2], V[2,3], V[1,3] and the decision.
steps: Write w = aab, n = 3. CNF rules: S→AB, A→AA, A→a, B→b.
V[1,2] for aa: split k=1 gives {A} and {A}; A→AA adds A, so V[1,2]={A}.
V[2,3] for ab: split k=2 gives {A} and {B}; S→AB adds S, so V[2,3]={S}.
V[1,3] for aab: k=1 gives {A} and {S}; no rule. k=2 gives {A} and {B}; S→AB adds S, so V[1,3]={S}.
examples.answer: For w = aab, n = 3, the table has 6 cells, V[1,3] = {S}, so aab ∈ L(G) (accepted = 1).

traps: Running CYK on a non-CNF grammar. Mixed rules such as A→aB are skipped; convert first (3.5).
Filling row by row left to right. Fill all shorter lengths before longer ones; otherwise needed cells are empty.
Putting one variable in a cell. Put a set; different variables can derive the same substring.
Taking the last filled cell as the answer. Read V[1,n].
Forgetting the terminal base case. A variable enters V[i,i] only when its rule gives exactly s[i].

quiz.q: Which normal form does CYK need?
Why fill by increasing substring length?
quiz.a: Each cell uses only shorter substrings, which must be ready.

quiz.q: S→AB, A→a, B→b, w=ab. Give V[1,1], V[2,2], V[1,2], decision.
quiz.a: V[1,1]={A}, V[2,2]={B}; split k=1 with A,B gives S; V[1,2]={S}; accept.
Several variables can derive the same substring; one rule may need any of them.

quiz.q: n=4, |P|=10. Give cells and worst-case rule checks.
quiz.a: Cells = n(n+1)/2 = 10. Split points = 10, rules = 10, so 100 rule checks; the asymptotic bound is O(n³·|P|), which for n = 4 and |P| = 10 is at most 640.

quiz.q: What goes wrong with rule A→aB?
quiz.a: Not CNF; CYK skips it, so convert first or the answer may be wrong.

beyond: Not for the exam. CYK is the classic O(n³) recognition algorithm. Faster in practice, not in the worst case: Earley and GLR also take O(n³) on general grammars, but they avoid the CNF conversion and run in O(n²) or O(n) for many real grammars, which is why compilers use them. The same table idea appears in RNA secondary-structure folding, where substrings combine into larger structures. Probabilistic CYK is used in statistical parsing and speech tagging. Search for 'CYK algorithm dynamic programming' and 'probabilistic CYK'.
